rows.selection_reason: With no prior evidence, the most critical uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion actually adds value over a strong unimodal baseline. Config_002 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is the simplest possible RNA-only configuration—no fusion, no aggregation, single profile—making it a clean reference floor. scvi_n200 is a well-established, robust single-cell RNA encoder, so this experiment isolates the question 'How well can we classify using RNA alone?' without confounding variables. Establishing this baseline first is essential: any subsequent multimodal result can only be interpreted as a gain (or lack thereof) relative to this number. It directly operationalizes the principle of not assuming complex multimodal models will outperform simpler ones, and it reduces the greatest uncertainty in the search space before investing experiments in more complex configurations.

We have only one completed experiment (config_002: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200 → Acc 0.520), so the most critical uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit over the RNA-only baseline. config_051 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting identical to config_002 and introduces only the image modality with a simple concat fusion, thereby isolating the effect of adding image information. This is the cleanest possible A/B comparison: any performance difference directly attributes to the image channel rather than confounds from a different encoder, profile setting, or aggregation scheme. Under a limited budget, establishing whether multimodality helps at all is the highest-value information to obtain before investing in more complex multiprofile or aggregation variants.

We have RNA-only (config_002: acc 0.520) and multimodal (config_051: acc 0.532) results, but no image-only baseline. The ~1.2% multimodal improvement is small and its source is ambiguous: the image may be contributing genuine signal, or the model may be relying primarily on RNA with the image adding noise. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) directly complements config_002 to complete the single-modality baseline pair, isolating the image encoder's independent predictive power. This is the highest-information experiment under budget because: (1) it clarifies whether the image modality is worth investing further experiments in, (2) it tells us whether the small multimodal gain reflects real complementary information or a marginal effect, and (3) it is a clean single-variable comparison (swap RNA→image) that avoids confounding with profile, aggregation, or fusion changes. Without this baseline, subsequent multiprofile or aggregation experiments would be harder to interpret.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieves 0.5203 acc, and config_051 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) improves to 0.5321 acc / 0.5172 F1, showing a modest but consistent multimodal gain. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.2266), confirming RNA dominates. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the concat fusion in config_051 is optimal or whether a weighted fusion would better calibrate the contribution of the weak image signal. This experiment (config_038) changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and profile setting identical to config_051, providing a clean single-variable A/B test. If weighted fusion outperforms concat, it indicates the image branch is noisy and should be downweighted, directly informing all future multimodal designs. If concat remains better, the image signal is additive and the fusion choice is less critical. Under a tight budget, isolating this one design decision from the already-validated baseline is the most informative next step before exploring additional axes (image encoder, multiprofile, RNA encoder).

All four completed experiments are singleprofile, so we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile + aggregation improves performance. The best result so far is config_038 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, acc=0.537). config_045 is the minimal, controlled extension of that best result: it keeps the same model setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion method, and only changes profile_setting from single to multi with avgpool aggregation (which is inherent to multiprofile). This directly tests whether representing each cell with multiple profiles and aggregating them (vs. a single profile) yields a meaningful gain. If multiprofile helps, it opens a large and promising sub-space; if it does not, we can confidently prune all multiprofile configurations and focus remaining budget on RNA/image encoder and fusion refinements within singleprofile. Under a tight budget, resolving this high-impact binary question with a one-axis change from our current best is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: config_045 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clear outlier at 0.706 acc, far exceeding the singleprofile multimodal configs (~0.53–0.54). The dominant driver is the multiprofile setting with aggregation. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the simple avgpool aggregation is near-optimal or whether a more expressive transformer aggregation could capture inter-profile interactions and push performance higher. This experiment (config_043) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other parameters identical to config_045 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile). It cleanly isolates the aggregation effect in the multiprofile regime. Under a limited budget, this is the best next step because it directly tests the most impactful potential improvement to our current best configuration; a positive result would justify further aggregation exploration, while a null result would confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect effort toward encoder or fusion choices.

The current best (config_043: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc. The single most important untested design variable is the RNA encoder in the multiprofile/transformer setting, since all completed multiprofile experiments used scvi_n200. config_046 swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 while holding image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. This isolates whether a learned nonlinear representation (scvi) is meaningfully better than a linear PCA projection for the RNA modality when profiles are aggregated by a transformer. If pca_n2000 performs comparably, the RNA encoder is not a bottleneck and we can redirect budget to other variables (e.g., image encoder or fusion); if it degrades substantially, scvi's learned representation is confirmed as critical. This single-variable comparison from the current best is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

The largest performance jump in the history (0.537→0.725) came from switching to multiprofile, but we cannot yet tell how much of that gain is driven by the multiprofile aggregation itself versus the multimodal combination. config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-factor ablation of the image modality from the current best config_043. If RNA-only multiprofile approaches ~0.70, the image adds little and future effort should target RNA encoders (e.g., scgpt). If it drops substantially (e.g., below 0.60), the image is essential and we should explore image-encoder variants (resnet50) and fusion strategies. This single experiment resolves a major design uncertainty that will determine the direction of all subsequent experiments, making it the highest-information-use choice under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_043: multiprofile, transformer, weighted, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l) achieves 0.725 accuracy, and the single most impactful finding is that multiprofile+transformer aggregation drives most of the gain. However, we have only tested 'weighted' fusion in this critical setting; the single-profile experiments showed weighted marginally beating concat (0.537 vs 0.532), but that gap was tiny and the dynamics may differ when a transformer aggregation produces richer multi-profile representations. Config_047 changes exactly one variable (fusion: weighted→concat) from our best config, cleanly isolating the fusion effect. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it either confirms that weighted fusion is optimal (reducing the search space) or reveals a meaningful gain from concat in the multiprofile+transformer regime, directly informing whether further optimization should focus on fusion architecture or other components.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc. We have strong evidence that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + scvi_n200 are critical, and that weighted ≈ concat for fusion. However, the image encoder dimension is essentially unexplored in the multiprofile multimodal regime—we have only tested imagenet_vit_l. Image-only performance is very weak (0.227), yet the image modality adds ~7 points over RNA-only in the multimodal setting, so the specific image architecture may matter. Question: config_018 changes only the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50 while holding all other settings at their best-performing values (scvi_n200, transformer, weighted, multiprofile). This isolates the effect of image encoder architecture. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the current best, it probes the least-understood design axis (image encoder choice in the multiprofile setting), and the result will tell us whether the ViT-specific features are important or whether a standard CNN backbone is sufficient—information that is critical for both further model search and practical deployment, and that cannot be inferred from any existing experiment.
